rv.q: Ethically knotty exploration of protest and powerlessness
The play illustrates, with believable characters, the way grief can turn into anger, which in turn can sometimes shift uneasily between taking protest action and despair.
The politics of policing protest have left the building along with the sharper dialogue of the middle section of the play, melodrama, regrettably, crowding out drama.
Fire Fire is certainly a memorable theatrical experience commencing in conflict, ending in connection, fuelled by climate change, packed with cleverly crafted characters and laced with comedy.
Fire Fire is an impressively crafted production... the play does not reduce climate action to a simple question of right and wrong.

The play as it stands is either too short or too long: not as concept, but when you pack in prison like a lighthouse flash and the gathering crescendo with accelerated narrative, the weight of it can evaporate.
A slickly produced production, but a play that never quite sorts its focus.
The initial sparks burnt brightly but quickly and could not fuel the fire for the full running time.
All in all, there is clear writing talent here but too many un-focussed ideas do not a great play make - and this never catches fire.
The result can feel emotionally tiring rather than increasingly affecting.

cn.t: Webber's climate activism drama divides critics with its timely subject matter and strong performances, but an unfocused script prevents it from fully igniting. The two-hander sustains urgency while exploring class tensions, yet struggles to overcome structural issues.
